source.title: Factual Inconsistency in Data-to-Text Generation Scales Exponentially with LLM Size: A Statistical Validation
source.authors: Joy Mahapatra; Soumyajit Roy; U. Garain

page_placements.theme: Task structure and metric choice determine additional scaling forms

record.tranche_reason: The study compares scaling forms for factual inconsistency in fine-tuned data-to-text generation, not the held-out pretraining loss, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling results for factual inconsistency, a different measure from held-out pretraining loss. Those results are recorded with versions ["none"] and described under fits_no_version. The paper also cites earlier scaling-law results, which are not recorded as findings from this study.
record.test_reason: Factual inconsistency on fine-tuned data-to-text tasks is a downstream performance measure. The study fits how it changes with model size across three families and checks those fits on held-out data, so its results bear on V6 (downstream predictability with scale) in a new setting. It does not measure pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. Its finding that exponential fits beat power-law fits concerns the functional form of a downstream metric, which no version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that factual inconsistency in QLoRA fine-tuned data-to-text generation generally follows exponential rather than power-law scaling with model size, declining rapidly up to about 3–4B parameters and then stabilising. They treat BLOOM exceptions as outliers due to few models, and acknowledge reliance on automatic metrics and non-universal parameters. The paraphrase should also mention that deterministic decoding on E2E and ViGGO shows inconsistency rising with size.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits power-law and exponential functions to factual-inconsistency scores after QLoRA fine-tuning on D2T datasets, rather than measuring held-out pretraining cross-entropy or compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported results vary with metric, dataset, model family, and decoding strategy. The appendix reports anomalous increases in inconsistency with size for some E2E and ViGGO deterministic-decoding settings.

fits_no_version.finding: In QLoRA fine-tuned data-to-text generation, factual inconsistency versus model size is generally better fit by an exponential than a power law (Vuong test, p<0.005). Exceptions: OPT on ViGGO (AlignScore) and BLOOM on WikiTableText (UniEval).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream factual inconsistency in fine-tuned data-to-text follows an exponential, not a power-law, dependence on model size.

record.problems: The authors report empirical results only, no theoretical guarantee; they use automated consistency metrics without direct human evaluation; scaling parameters may not transfer across datasets and architectures. Some BLOOM results fail goodness-of-fit, and the paper notes larger margins of error in some settings.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many separate family-by-dataset-by-metric comparisons and additional decoding-strategy results in Appendix A. The four rows retain the authors' aggregate main-text findings, not each tabulated cell or appendix condition.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, data or compute.
Extrapolation to much larger runs. Predictive checks are five-fold cross-validation within the 70M–13B range.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens.
Architecture shape at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law form of loss in other modalities or regimes. QLoRA is used, but loss is not modelled.
Predictability from pretraining loss. Only parameter count is used, across families that differ in data and training.
Fit-dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or of the compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Inconsistency increases with model size under greedy and beam-search decoding on E2E and ViGGO (reversed direction).
Per-cell results for greedy, beam and top-k decoding, including frequent goodness-of-fit failures in BLOOM and OPT.
Exponential rate β falls between −1.8 and −0.6 where the margin of error is not high; decline plateaus after about 3–4B parameters.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6 tag treats the study as outside the claim. But factual inconsistency on downstream tasks versus scale falls under V6, so it is reclassified as T3 for V6 only. Caveats: model size is compared across checkpoints of existing pretrained families that differ in data and training, not under controlled scaling. 'Predictive performance' is within-range cross-validation on 5–8 points per family, not extrapolation. Table 1 lists the smallest BLOOM model as '0.56M', presumably 560M.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs' held-out pretraining loss from small runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens.
Effects of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study uses QLoRA fine-tuning, but tests scaling of factual inconsistency rather than the power-law form of held-out loss in another training regime or modality.
Downstream task performance or its predictability from pretraining loss.
Whether exponents or compute-optimal allocation for held-out pretraining loss depend on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: Pythia, OPT, and BLOOM families (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Pythia: 70M–12B; OPT: 130M–13B; BLOOM: Table 1 lists 0.56M, 1.1B, 1.7B, 3B, and 7B
rows.stage_stated: QLoRA fine-tuned separately on D2T datasets
rows.operation_detail: Fits and compares power-law and exponential scaling of factual inconsistency against model size.
rows.measure: Factual inconsistency (1 − factual consistency); scaling-model validation and preference
rows.value: The authors report that exponential scaling is generally preferred; Table 2 marks exceptions, including ViGGO with OPT.
rows.uncertainty: Figures report 95% confidence intervals on residuals; no interval values stated in the text.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the reported family-by-dataset comparisons; it concerns factual inconsistency, not held-out pretraining loss.
rows.check: Versions should include V6. Under nucleus sampling, AlignScore inconsistency falls with size and both fits have low held-out Huber loss. Both laws pass goodness-of-fit for Pythia and OPT; BLOOM fails in some cells (Table 2). The 'value' describes which law is preferred, which is not itself a V6 effect.

source_check.correct: The value summary is supported. However, OPT WikiTableText held-out Huber losses are 2.82e+03 for exponential and 6.37e+01 for power law; OPT ViGGO favors power law.
source_check.problem: The attached verdict-fix comment incorrectly describes both fits as having low held-out loss without the OPT WikiTableText exception.

relationships.condition: Pythia and OPT families, stochastic decoding (nucleus; top-k in the appendix), all four metrics
relationships.reason: Inconsistency falls with size; fits pass goodness-of-fit and have low held-out Huber loss in nearly all cells (r1–r4).
relationships.display_finding: Inconsistency generally decreased with size, but OPT WikiTableText had large held-out losses for AlignScore and SummaC-Conv fits under nucleus sampling and for exponential fits under top-k sampling.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Pythia and OPT families, stochastic decoding (nucleus; top-k in the appendix), all four metrics
source_check.reason: This condition group mixes successful predictions with substantial failures. For nucleus sampling, OPT WikiTableText has enormous held-out losses for both AlignScore fits (Table 2) and both SummaC-Conv fits (Table 4). Top-k exponential fits also have high OPT WikiTableText losses (Tables 14 and 16). Narrow supports to successful cells and separately qualify these exceptions.

relationships.condition: BLOOM family (five models), QAFactEval and SummaC-Conv
relationships.reason: Neither scaling law passes the F-test in most BLOOM dataset cells, so the trend is not reliably predictable there (r2, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Neither tested scaling law passed the F-test in most BLOOM dataset and metric combinations.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: BLOOM family (five models), QAFactEval and SummaC-Conv
source_check.reason: Under nucleus sampling, both laws fail goodness-of-fit on BLOOM DART, E2E and WikiTableText for QAFactEval, and DART, E2E and ViGGO for SummaC-Conv (r2–r3; Tables 3–4).

relationships.reason: The authors read the exponential fits as a rapid decline up to about 3–4B parameters, then stabilisation. Improvement plateaus rather than continuing (Section 7 text; aggregate across r1–r4).
relationships.display_finding: The fitted exponential curves indicated rapid inconsistency reductions up to roughly 3–4B parameters, followed by stabilization.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Section 7 interprets the fitted exponential curves as declining rapidly and then stabilizing. Predictable saturation alone does not establish a failure of V6, which specifies neither a power-law form nor sustained gains of a particular magnitude.

relationships.display_finding: Factual inconsistency increased with model size under greedy and beam-search decoding, mainly for OPT and BLOOM.
